1.pericope_label: Also, thou son of man, prophesy unto the mountains of Israel, and say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord: Thus saith the Lord God; Because the enemy hath said against you, Aha, even the ancient high places are ours in possession: Therefore prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord God; Because they have made you desolate, and swallowed you up on every side, that ye might be a possession unto the residue of the heathen, and ye are taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people: Therefore, ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord God; Thus saith the Lord God to the mountains, and to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys, to the desolate wastes, and to the cities that are forsaken, which became a prey and derision to the residue of the heathen that are round about; Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Surely in the fire of my jealousy have I spoken against the residue of the heathen, and against all Idumea, which have appointed my land into their possession with the joy of all their heart, with despiteful minds, to cast it out for a prey. Prophesy therefore concerning the land of Israel, and say unto the mountains, and to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys, Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I have spoken in my jealousy and in my fury, because ye have borne the shame of the heathen: Therefore thus saith the Lord God; I have lifted up mine hand, Surely the heathen that are about you, they shall bear their shame. But ye, O mountains of Israel, ye shall shoot forth your branches, and yield your fruit to my people of Israel; for they are at hand to come. For, behold, I am for you, and I will turn unto you, and ye shall be tilled and sown: And I will multiply men upon you, all the house of Israel, even all of it: and the cities shall be inhabited, and the wastes shall be builded: And I will multiply upon you man and beast; and they shall increase and bring fruit: and I will settle you after your old estates, and will do better unto you than at your beginnings: and ye shall know that I am the Lord. Yea, I will cause men to walk upon you, even my people Israel; and they shall possess thee, and thou shalt be their inheritance, and thou shalt no more henceforth bereave them of men. Thus saith the Lord God; Because they say unto you, Thou land devourest up men, and hast bereaved thy nations; Therefore thou shalt devour men no more, neither bereave thy nations any more, saith the Lord God. Neither will I cause men to hear in thee the shame of the heathen any more, neither shalt thou bear the reproach of the people any more, neither shalt thou cause thy nations to fall any more, saith the Lord God.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the enemy's boast flatly, that the everlasting heights have fallen to them for a possession and Israel has come into the talk of the tongue; Ellicott explains that mountains here stand for land and people together and hold the contrast with the mountain named in the oracle just before, reads the phrase about ancient high places as an allusion to the everlasting hills of two old blessings, takes the enemy as a general term for the heathen at large rather than for Edom alone, since the surrounding nations saw the land desolate and concluded that the promise had failed, corrects swallowed up to pant for as a word drawn from the snuffing of wild beasts, prefers empty out to cast out, notes that the lifted hand means swearing and that the reproach Israel carried now turns back on those who inflicted it, hears both certainty and nearness in the command to bear fruit, grants only a partial fulfilment after the exile and in the Maccabean age while finding the language outrun the history, traces the reproach that the land devours its people to the old spies' report, and closes by observing a wordplay English cannot carry and by arguing that a prophecy assuming an Edom still standing cannot be waiting on a literal future fulfilment.

Gill takes the mountains for the hill country of Judah and prefers concerning to against, since these later oracles are in their favour, notes that the country being cleared of men there was nothing left to speak to, grounds the fire of jealousy in the cruelty of the neighbours' conduct, and has the mountains tilled and sown, men multiplied, and the beasts restored.

Clarke calls the address a beautiful personification, identifies the enemy specifically as the Edomites, who had seized the high ground and its fortresses during the captivity to shut the Jews out if they returned, and presses the nearness of the restoration, saying it was so determined that one might be as sure of it as if the families were crossing the border, though some fifty-eight of the seventy years were still to run, while doubting, with another writer, that the promise to do better than at the beginning can be shown fulfilled between the return and the birth of Christ, the colouring being too high and the whole suiting gospel times better; Wesley allows many enemies but says they conspired so far that the prophet treats them as one, calls the lifted hand swearing in wrath, names the three neighbouring peoples, and answers the reproach with the blessing that the country will raise sons and daughters and the reproach cease.

Henry observes that the prophet had once been sent against these same hills and must now speak comfortably to them, the people being gone and the ground alone left, which the conquerors could not carry away, and supplies the scene behind the boast, the neighbours flying to the spoil as to a shipwreck with nobody thinking it a crime to strip an Israelite, so that neither antiquity nor sanctity nor fortification had saved the place.

debates.question: Who is the enemy that boasts over the mountains?

positions.position: The Edomites specifically, who had seized the high ground and its fortresses during the captivity.
Many enemies conspiring so far in one design that the prophet speaks of them as one.
The heathen at large: the term is general, and the following verses point to all the surrounding nations, who took the desolation for proof that the promise had failed.

debates.question: How far can the promise of doing better than at the beginning be taken literally?

positions.position: Not literally at all for the period after the return; the colouring is too high and the whole suits gospel times better.
Partially fulfilled after the exile and in the Maccabean age, but the language outruns the history, so the earthly blessings become shadow and type.
Literally enough as agriculture and population, the mountains tilled and sown, men multiplied and the beasts restored.

outliers.claim: Argues that since the prophecy assumes an Edom still standing and still gloating, it cannot be awaiting a literal future fulfilment, that nation having long since disappeared and no later people being able to stand in its historic place.
Points out that the ground is addressed precisely because it is all that was left, the people having been carried off and the land being the one thing the conquerors could not take with them.

16.pericope_label: Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, when the house of Israel dwelt in their own land, they defiled it by their own way and by their doings: their way was before me as the uncleanness of a removed woman. Wherefore I poured my fury upon them for the blood that they had shed upon the land, and for their idols wherewith they had polluted it: And I scattered them among the heathen, and they were dispersed through the countries: according to their way and according to their doings I judged them. And when they entered unto the heathen, whither they went, they profaned my holy name, when they said to them, These are the people of the Lord, and are gone forth out of his land. But I had pity for mine holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the heathen, whither they went. Therefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord God; I do not this for your sakes, O house of Israel, but for mine holy name’s sake, which ye have profaned among the heathen, whither ye went. And I will sanctify my great name, which was profaned among the heathen, which ye have profaned in the midst of them; and the heathen shall know that I am the Lord, saith the Lord God, when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set out the whole argument of the new oracle before commenting on any part of it, that Israel defiled its land and was scattered for it, but that because the scattering profaned God's name among the nations he will act for that name's sake, gathering, cleansing and sanctifying them by the gift of his Spirit and then blessing them until both the nations and Israel know who he is; they treat the opening formula as marking an independent word bound to what precedes as the motive of the restoration, and locate its kernel in the promise of clean water and a new heart. Ellicott supplies the principle that the land is consecrated ground which the people's sin defiles, identifies the comparison with a woman set apart for uncleanness and kept from the sanctuary until her purifying, argues that the name was profaned not chiefly by the exiles' conduct but by the bare fact of captivity, since the heathen took their God for a national one and concluded he had been unable to protect his people, and ends on the textual variant between in your eyes and in their eyes, preferring the first because it brings out that God must be sanctified in the eyes of his own people before he can be sanctified through them in anyone else's.

Gill notes that a fresh prophecy begins here, describes what was lost as a land of plenty also chosen for God's worship, makes the pity a concern for God's own honour rather than for the people's, and takes the sanctifying of the name as clearing it of the charges laid against it, observing that God chose to vindicate it by grace rather than by the punishment he might justly have inflicted.

Clarke states the counterfactual, that had they stayed faithful they would never have been removed, but they polluted the land and God gave up land and people to the destroyers, has the exiles so fallen that God was blasphemed on their account with onlookers asking what being could own such a people, and locates the demonstration of holiness in the people themselves, since changing their hearts and conduct is how God shows his hatred of vice and love of holiness; Wesley reads the figure of uncleanness as exclusion from the congregation for some great sin, puts the taunt in the neighbours' mouths, says the sins deserved cutting off but that destroying them would have let the heathen draw conclusions against God's power and truth, and holds that they had given the heathen occasion to think meanly of him and he will show himself as great as good.

Henry says the land had the eye of God upon it and presses the phrase their own way as meaning the way of their own choosing, so that the blame is theirs, and reaches the doctrine from the captives' side, that their unworthiness was the discouragement and the answer is that God acts for his own name, the restoration being a type of redemption whose every step ends in the glory of God.

debates.question: How did the exiles profane God's name among the nations?

positions.position: By their conduct, being so fallen that God was blasphemed on their account and onlookers asked what being could own such a people.
By the bare fact of their captivity: the heathen took their God for a merely national one and concluded from the dispersion that he could not protect them.
By the taunt it put in their neighbours' mouths, that these slaves call themselves the people of the Lord and claim a land they were driven out of.

debates.question: In whose eyes must God be sanctified first?

positions.position: The Hebrew as it stands reads in your eyes, and that reading is preferable, since God must be sanctified in his own people by their repentance before he can be sanctified through them in anyone else's.
In the people, since changing their hearts and conduct is the demonstration of God's hatred of vice and love of holiness.
In the name itself, cleared of the charges laid against it and vindicated by grace rather than by deserved punishment.

outliers.claim: Turns the refusal to act for Israel's sake against a modern objection, arguing that a narrative which repeatedly sets aside the mass of a chosen nation and purifies a remnant for a purpose reaching the whole world is unlike any other national legend.
Reads the oracle as a single argument whose kernel is the promise of clean water and a new heart, everything before it preparing the way and everything after it drawing the consequence.

24.pericope_label: For I will take you from among the heathen, and gather you out of all countries, and will bring you into your own land. Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them. And ye shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers; and ye shall be my people, and I will be your God.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears a priest speaking when the clean water is promised, referring to the washings of the law in their symbolic force rather than to any one of them, with the primary reference to cleansing from idolatry and to the people as a body though what follows requires it to reach individuals too, and observes that the same symbolism later produced the washing of proselytes, taken up by the forerunner and made the initiatory sacrament; on the new heart he notes that the promise stood earlier in the book in shorter form, and on the promise of the land he explains why an earthly promise is still needed, since the people could not yet seek spiritual good except as attached to temporal good, the temporal being in providence the necessary means to the spiritual, so that the restoration had to be promised and in due time literally given.

Gill has the people fetched out of the nations they were carried to and those they live among still, the work completed at the conversion of the Jews in the latter day, and reads the phrase besides as an image of grace calling a people out of the world; he argues at length that the clean water is not baptism, as one father held, since baptism is not performed by sprinkling and is administered by men rather than being an operation of God, nor the renewing grace of the Spirit, which the next verse covers, and settles on the blood of Christ; he treats heart and spirit as one thing renewed, carrying a new principle of life, a new will, and affections that bring new sorrows as well as new delights; and he values the land as a gift promised to the fathers, so that its restoration proves the promise was not forgotten.

Clarke denies that the gathering relates to the return from Babylon, since the Jews are scattered to this day through heathen, Muslim and Christian countries alike, makes the clean water the influences of the Spirit with the filthiness covering every pollution outward and inward and the idols false worship, false opinions and false hopes alike, divides heart from spirit by giving the one the affections and the other the mind, understanding, judgment and will, is severe on the stony heart as hard, impenetrable and cold, frozen to good and slow to credit God's words and taken away entire since nobody holds the new heart and the old at once, builds a hierarchy in which the Spirit actuates the new spirit and that the new affections so that passion is ruled by reason and reason by the Spirit, presses that the cause is evidenced by the effect since walking in the statutes means conduct actually regulated by them, and calls this the birthright of every believer rather than a promise to Israel only; Wesley describes a frame moulded into compliance with the whole will of God, taking the impress as soft wax takes a seal, leaves the will its part by insisting that the causing is sweet and powerful yet without compulsion because a spirit already framed to a disposition suitable to God's holiness readily concurs, marks the order and will not have it reversed, that then and not before are these promises to be fulfilled, and calls the covenant formula the foundation of the top-stone of a believer's happiness.

Henry keeps both senses of the sprinkling at once, the blood applied to the conscience as the water of purification removed a ceremonial stain, and the grace of the Spirit sprinkled on the whole soul.

debates.question: What is the clean water that is sprinkled?

positions.position: The blood of Christ, and expressly not baptism, which is not by sprinkling and is administered by men, nor the Spirit's renewing grace, which the next verse covers.
The influences of the Holy Spirit, of which water is the natural type.
The washings of the law taken together in their symbolic force, the same symbolism that later produced the washing of proselytes and then baptism.
Both at once: blood on the conscience and the Spirit's grace on the whole soul.

debates.question: How does the promised Spirit produce obedience?

positions.position: Through a hierarchy of causes, the Spirit actuating the new spirit and that the affections, so that passion is ruled by reason and reason by the Spirit, with conduct as the evidence.
Sweetly and powerfully yet without compulsion, since a spirit already framed to a disposition suitable to God's holiness readily concurs.

outliers.claim: Explains why an earthly promise is still required at this point, since the people could not yet seek spiritual good except as attached to temporal good, which providence made the necessary means to it.
Insists that the whole promise is the birthright of every believer and not a prediction about Israel only, the complete destruction of sin in the soul being what is offered.

themes: For I will take you from among the heathen, and gather you out of all countries, and will bring you into your own land.
Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.

29.pericope_label: I will also save you from all your uncleannesses: and I will call for the corn, and will increase it, and lay no famine upon you. And I will multiply the fruit of the tree, and the increase of the field, that ye shall receive no more reproach of famine among the heathen. Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that were not good, and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations. Not for your sakes do I this, saith the Lord God, be it known unto you: be ashamed and confounded for your own ways, O house of Israel. Thus saith the Lord God; In the day that I shall have cleansed you from all your iniquities I will also cause you to dwell in the cities, and the wastes shall be builded. And the desolate land shall be tilled, whereas it lay desolate in the sight of all that passed by. And they shall say, This land that was desolate is become like the garden of Eden; and the waste and desolate and ruined cities are become fenced, and are inhabited. Then the heathen that are left round about you shall know that I the Lord build the ruined places, and plant that that was desolate: I the Lord have spoken it, and I will do it. Thus saith the Lord God; I will yet for this be enquired of by the house of Israel, to do it for them; I will increase them with men like a flock. As the holy flock, as the flock of Jerusalem in her solemn feasts; so shall the waste cities be filled with flocks of men: and they shall know that I am the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott asks why a further cleansing should be promised when the people have already been washed and given a new heart, and answers that it cannot be the idolatry already purged away but is plain if taken for the ordinary sinfulness of a man, continually renewed and so needing continual forgiveness; he weighs the comparison with the garden of Eden, allowing that it may mean no more than that the land became prosperous but preferring, in the light of what precedes, a condition in which man is once more wholly free of sin, the state the church has prepared for in every age; he finds the point of God's being inquired of in the contrast with earlier chapters, where God refused to be inquired of by a people whose heart was far from him; and he agrees that the flocks give a vivid idea of numbers while noting an added fitness in the figure, those flocks being devoted to the Lord.

Gill distinguishes deliverance from the dominion of sin by grace and from its guilt by the blood, reads the promised plenty on two levels as orchard and field literally and the increase of gifts in the churches spiritually, catalogues what the restored people will remember, the breaches of the law before the exile and the self-made righteousness after, observes that the goodness of God is what refreshes the memory so that sins never counted sins return with all their weight, is blunt that God acts on no merit but only grace, has the waste ground made fruitful again and offers beside it the fallow ground of the heart ploughed and sown, states plainly that God has promised and will perform yet expects his people to apply to him and plead the promise, records a reading of the versions that reverses the direction and makes God the seeker of Israel, and takes the closing figure from the animals consecrated for sacrifice and driven up to the city at the annual feasts.

Clarke puts to himself the objection the passage invites, whether people saved so far will not grow proud and undervalue the blood once they no longer need it, and answers from the verse about self-loathing that such people never forget the pit they came out of, never forgive themselves for sinning against so good a God, and find the blood more precious than ever, since it takes the same power to sustain a creation as to make one and the same Christ to keep clean who cleansed; he compresses the restoration into a sentence, that a land desolate by sin becomes like the garden of Eden by righteousness, turns the verse about inquiry into an answer to who shall have such blessings, and ends with a declaration he refuses to apologise for, that he has read the chapter throughout of the redemption under the new covenant and not of the return from Babylon; Wesley reads the tense of the salvation as continuous and packs into it justification, entire sanctification and fitness for glory, holds that a repeated promise does not excuse anyone from asking, and presses that increase of population is honourable only where the people are dedicated as a holy flock.

debates.question: Why is a further cleansing promised after the new heart has been given?

positions.position: Because it cannot mean the idolatry already purged; it is the ordinary sinfulness of man, continually renewed and needing continual forgiveness.
Because the salvation is continuous, and takes in justification, entire sanctification, and fitness for glory together.
Because deliverance from the dominion of sin by grace is distinct from deliverance from its guilt by the blood.

debates.question: Why must a people who have been promised everything still ask for it?

positions.position: Because God's promising and performing does not remove the duty of applying to him and pleading the promise; though one reading of the versions reverses the direction and makes God the seeker.
Because the verse answers the question who shall have such blessings: those who pray, seek earnestly, and strive to enter by the narrow gate.
Because the contrast is with earlier chapters, where God refused to be inquired of by a people whose heart was far from him and now, having given a new heart, hears.
Because however often a promise is repeated, it does not excuse anyone from asking.

outliers.claim: Refuses to apologise for reading the whole chapter of the redemption under the new covenant rather than the return from Babylon, on the ground that no period of the nation's history since answers to it.
Turns the closing simile into a rule about population, that increase of numbers is honourable only where the people are dedicated to God as a holy flock, crowds being a lovely sight in his temple.
